```{r}
#| label: setup
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)
tab_dir <- file.path("..", "results", "tables")
fig_dir <- file.path("..", "results", "figures")
k <- function(f, digits = 3) kable(
  read_csv(file.path(tab_dir, f), show_col_types = FALSE), digits = digits)
# Slim display for contrast tables: combine the HL estimate with its CI so
# wide tables fit a portrait page without wrapping.
fmt_contrast <- function(f) {
  d <- read_csv(file.path(tab_dir, f), show_col_types = FALSE)
  d$hl <- sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", d$hl_est, d$hl_l, d$hl_u)
  keep <- c("contrast", "n_pairs", "W", "p", "p_holm", "hl", "r_rb")
  keep <- keep[keep %in% names(d)]
  out <- d[, keep]
  names(out) <- c("Contrast", "n", "W", "p", "p (Holm)", "HL [95% CI]", "r")[seq_along(keep)]
  kable(out, digits = 4)
}
```

## Abstract

Methanolic extracts of *Azadirachta indica* and *Moringa oleifera* (leaves,
stem bark, roots, seeds) were tested against *Trypanosoma congolense* and
*T. evansi* in motility assays and in albino mice (N = 16 plant × part ×
parasite blocks; group means of n = 3 mice). Both parasites show a clear,
monotonic dose response: *T. evansi* significantly (parasitaemia Friedman
p = 0.006; top three doses beat control, Holm 0.039; motility Friedman
p < 0.001) and *T. congolense* suggestively (parasitaemia Friedman p = 0.074;
100 mg/ml Holm 0.071; motility Friedman p < 0.001 with post-hocs just above
threshold). At 100 mg/ml the mean peak parasitaemia is zero in both parasites
with no deaths, against peak LEV 5 and universal mortality in Negative
Controls. No evidence separates the two plants (paired p = 1.0, HL 0.3
[−14.7, 20.5]). All inference is block-level and rank-based; every headline
claim survived leave-one-block-out sensitivity analysis.

## 1. Aim, objectives and section map

The aim of this study is to comparatively evaluate the anti-trypanosomal
activity of methanolic extracts of the leaves, stem bark, roots and seeds of
*Azadirachta indica* and *Moringa oleifera* against *Trypanosoma congolense*
and *T. evansi* (thesis §1.8.1). Each specific objective (§1.8.2) is addressed
in a dedicated results section — extraction (i) in §5.1, phytochemical
characterisation (ii) in §5.2, the motility assay (iii) in §5.3, in-vivo
infectivity (iv) in §5.4, superiority (v) in §5.5 — each opening with
exploratory description before any inference, and each discussed jointly in
§7. Diagnostics, limitations and references follow in §6, §8 and §9.

## 2. Data and experimental design

Source data are group means of n = 3 mice per group, parsed from Sheet 2 of
the study workbook into tidy CSVs (`analysis/data/`, builder
`analysis/R/01_build_datasets.R`). Within any block each of the 7 groups is
therefore n = 1 (descriptive only); the analytical unit is the **block
(N = 16; 8 per plant, 8 per parasite)**. Plant contrasts pair by part ×
parasite (8 pairs); parasite contrasts pair by plant × part (8 pairs).
Controls appear as labelled in the source (identities/doses unstated), so the
Positive Control is an assay-validity reference only. A consequence of the
group-mean design, stressed throughout this report, is that no within-group
variance survives: every p-value below is computed over at most eight
paired blocks, power is low by construction, and effect sizes with confidence
intervals — not significance stars — are the primary read-out.

## 3. Endpoints

Parasitaemia (LEV 0–5 ordinal): primary **AUC** (death-censored trapezoid,
always with mortality), supported by peak LEV, clearance day and day-40
status — day-40 alone is degenerate (0/112 positive; positivity peaks ~30%
at days 9–14). Motility: TTI, t120, mean proportion motile (key: `+ Active`,
`− No motility`; `+-` → NA, 2 cells). Weight/PCV: Δ = Post − Pre with
literature flags (anaemia: Post < 35% or ≥ 25% drop, severe < 30%/≥ 40%;
weight signal ≥ 10% loss, severe ≥ 20%). Raw LEV > 5 (42 cells) capped to 5
with `lev_raw` preserved and flagged. Missing in-vivo values = death
(adopted convention, never imputed).

## 4. Statistical methods

Description first (trajectories, endpoint tables, flags), then rank-based
inference: Friedman blocked by block for dose trends with pooled Spearman ρ
on log10 dose; paired Wilcoxon signed-rank (exact when tie-free, otherwise
the continuity-corrected normal approximation — §6) for dose-vs-control
post-hocs and plant/parasite contrasts, with matched-pairs rank-biserial
effect size (|r| ≥ 0.11/0.28/0.43) and Hodges–Lehmann median difference with
95% CI. Dose-vs-control families are Holm-adjusted per parasite; plant and
parasite questions are independent and uncorrected across questions.
Per-block trend tests at n = 1 lack power, so only the blocked Friedman is
inferential. Significance p < 0.05, p-values supplementary to effects.
Script: `analysis/R/02_analysis.R` (statistics only, no ML).

## 5.1. Objective i — methanolic extraction

Objective i is a laboratory procedure with no statistical component — no
yields or replicates are recorded — so there is nothing to estimate or test.
It is noted here solely to keep the objective map complete; the statistical
story begins with the characterised extracts.

## 5.2. Objective ii — phytochemical contents

Exploration first. Screening recovered 8 of the 12 assayed classes in at
least one extract, with richness concentrated in leaves (6 of 12 in both
plants) and lowest in stem bark (*A. indica* 3, *M. oleifera* 4) and roots
(3 and 4); seeds sit in between (5 and 4) (@tbl-phyto; @fig-rich). Two
classes are universal — Saponin and Carbohydrates appear in all eight
plant × part combinations — and four are absent everywhere (Anthraquinone,
Phlobatanins, Oxalates, Phytates), so neither group discriminates the
plants. Tannins follow a striking part pattern, present everywhere except
seeds in both plants. The differentiating classes are few and part-specific:
Steroids occur only in *A. indica* leaves and seeds; Alkaloids in *M.
oleifera* leaves and roots plus *A. indica* leaves; Terpenoids solely in *M.
oleifera* stem bark; Flavonoids in the leaves and seeds of both plants; and
Glucosides in *M. oleifera* leaves and seeds but only *A. indica* seeds
(@fig-phyto-hm). Concretely, *A. indica* leaves carry Saponin, Steroid,
Alkaloid, Flavonoid, Tannins and Carbohydrates, while *M. oleifera* leaves
carry Saponin, Alkaloid, Flavonoid, Glucosides, Tannins and Carbohydrates —
the same richness (6/12) with Steroid/Glucosides swapped. With only eight
plant × part combinations no test has power, so inference stops here: the
matrix is the result, and compound–efficacy overlays are tabulated
exploratorily without tests (`phytochemical_efficacy_overlay.csv`). The
relevance for §7 is that the two plants' chemical arsenals overlap heavily
(universal Saponin/Carbohydrates/Tannins), which foreshadows the null
superiority finding — but with n = 8 this remains a consistency observation,
not a tested mediation.

k("phytochemical_richness.csv", 0)

## 5.3. Objective iii — in-vitro motility dose response

Exploration shows a textbook gradient. Median TTI rises monotonically as
concentration falls: 15 min at 100 mg/ml in both parasites with zero
censoring, 22–30 min at 10 mg/ml, 45–53 min at 0.5 mg/ml, 60–75 min at
0.01 mg/ml, 90–105 min at 0.005 mg/ml, and fully censored Negative Controls
(all 8 *evansi* NC groups never immobilise; 6 of 8 *congolense* NC groups
likewise), while mean t120 motility climbs from 0 at the top doses to 0.67
(*congolense* NC) and 1.0 (*evansi* NC) (@tbl-tti; @fig-tti). Trajectories
(@fig-mot-traj) confirm rapid kill at high doses — 100 mg/ml immobilises
within 15–30 minutes in most blocks — and validate the assay: the recovered
Positive Control rows show + at t = 0 and immobility thereafter in all 16
tables. Inference follows the description. The blocked dose trend is highly
significant for both parasites (@tbl-mot-dose: *congolense* Friedman
Q = 27.75, p < 0.001, pooled ρ = −0.70; *evansi* Q = 30.32, p < 0.001,
ρ = −0.88). Post-hoc dose-vs-control contrasts (@tbl-mot-posthoc) carry
large, consistent effects at the top doses — rank-biserial −1 throughout,
HL reductions of −0.83 (*congolense* 100 mg/ml, 95% CI [−0.94, −0.72]) and
−0.89 (*evansi* 100 mg/ml, [−0.94, −0.83]) — that sit just above
Holm-adjusted significance (0.065 and 0.052; 10 mg/ml: 0.085 and 0.052).
Lower doses are indistinguishable from the control (0.5 mg/ml Holm 0.17 and
0.064; 0.01/0.005 mg/ml ≥ 0.11), and several low-dose pairs have zero
differences (n_nonzero as low as 4 of 8), which is itself informative: weak
extracts match the control exactly. Heavy tied ranks (the endpoint averages
nine binary points) forced the asymptotic approximation in every motility
contrast — recorded per row — and conclusions are unchanged under it.

## 5.4. Objective iv — in-vivo infectivity

### Parasitaemia

Exploration first, because the numbers here are the backbone of the thesis.
Peak parasitaemia falls monotonically with dose in both parasites: at
100 mg/ml the mean peak is exactly zero across all eight blocks per
parasite with zero deaths, while Negative Controls peak at LEV 5 with
universal (100%) mortality (@tbl-peak; @fig-peak). The gradient is smooth —
*congolense* mean peaks 0 → 1.88 → 2.78 → 3.13 → 3.19 → 5.0 from 100 mg/ml
to control; *evansi* 0 → 0 → 0.63 → 1.93 → 2.08 → 5.0 — with mortality
tracking it (0% at top doses rising to 62–100% at low doses and control)
and median clearance days shortening as dose rises. Day-40 zeros accumulate
with dose (100% at top doses, 0% in controls), which together with the
zero-positive day-40 overall is why day-40 cannot carry inference.
Trajectories (@fig-para-traj) rise from day 1, peak near days 9–14 and
resolve in survivors, with deaths (44 of 112 groups) accompanying the
decline. Inference on cumulative burden (AUC) mirrors the peaks (@fig-auc):
monotonic in log-concentration, significant for *T. evansi* (@tbl-dose:
Friedman Q = 14.51, p = 0.006, pooled ρ = −0.51, mean per-block ρ = −0.86)
and suggestive for *T. congolense* (Q = 8.52, p = 0.074, ρ = −0.42, mean
per-block −0.46). Post-hocs (@tbl-para-posthoc) confirm *evansi* 100, 10
and 0.5 mg/ml, each beating the control in all eight blocks (W = 0, exact
p = 0.008, Holm 0.039; HL ≈ −50/−50/−44 AUC-days with lower limits near −75),
while 0.01 and 0.005 mg/ml do not survive correction (Holm 0.078 each, with
HL point estimates still strongly negative at −32/−34). For *T. congolense*
only 100 mg/ml is suggestive (asymptotic p = 0.014 — ties present — Holm
0.071, HL −29.9 [−41.0, −20.9], r = −1); every lower dose is far from
significance (Holm 0.32–0.73) despite negative point estimates. No
parasite-level AUC difference exists (paired W = 24, exact p = 0.46,
HL 6.0 [−10.7, 21.1], r = 0.25; @tbl-other) — the parasites differ in
*dose sensitivity*, not in overall burden.

### Body weight and PCV

Exploration: mean weight and PCV paths across Pre, Infection and Post run
roughly flat for both plants and parasites (@fig-wp-traj) — there is no
visible separation of trajectories by treatment — and deltas centre near
zero with wide scatter (@fig-wt, @fig-pcv). The flags tell the real story
(@tbl-flags): missingness (death) concentrates in *T. congolense* (7 + 3
weight groups, 7 + 3 PCV groups across the two plants, vs 1 each for *A.
indica*/*evansi* and none for *M. oleifera*/*evansi* weight); severe weight
loss (≥ 20%) hits 4 + 2 *congolense* groups plus one *A. indica*/*evansi*
group, with toxicity-signal (≥ 10%) flags in 4 + 4 *congolense* and 2 *A.
indica*/*evansi* groups; anaemia flags likewise cluster in *congolense*
(5 + 4 groups) with only 2 in *M. oleifera*/*evansi* and 2 severe-anaemia
flags in *A. indica*/*evansi*. Inference finds no plant or parasite signals
in the deltas (@tbl-other: weight plant W = 10, exact p = 0.31, HL −0.81
[−2.29, 0.44], r = 0; weight parasite W = 7, p = 0.15, HL −1.34
[−3.90, 0.29], r = −0.50; PCV plant W = 21, p = 0.74, HL 0.48
[−3.70, 4.38], r = 0.25; PCV parasite W = 19, p = 0.95, HL 0.40
[−3.62, 3.48], r = 0). Read together — flat trajectories, null delta tests,
but flags concentrated in *congolense* — efficacy in this study is
parasitological rather than confounded by differential toxicity, while
*T. congolense* remains the more pathogenic organism regardless of extract.

## 5.5. Objective v — comparative superiority

Exploration first: per-pair AUC differences (@fig-forest) scatter on both
sides of zero in both parasites — leaves/*congolense* −21.5 and
seeds/*evansi* −19.6 favour *M. oleifera* (negative = lower burden under
*M. oleifera*), while stem bark/*evansi* +18.1, roots/*evansi* +11.3 and
leaves/*evansi* +9.9 favour *A. indica*; roots/*congolense* (+4.0), stem
bark/*congolense* (−3.6) and seeds/*congolense* (exactly 0.0) sit near zero.
No pattern by part or parasite emerges, and the scatter (@fig-paired)
straddles identity. Inference confirms the visual: paired W = 14 on seven
non-zero differences (one exact tie dropped), exact p = 1.0, HL ≈ 0.3 with
95% CI (−14.7, +20.5), rank-biserial −0.14 (@tbl-sup); the motility
cross-check agrees (W = 29, exact p = 0.15, HL 0.11 [−0.08, 0.24],
r = 0.25). With eight pairs the interval spans meaningful effects in both
directions, so the data cannot support a superiority claim for either agent
— the honest conclusion is the null, stated with its interval rather than
as a bare p-value, and it is LOO-stable (sensitivity p-range 0.53–1.0, §6).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sup
#| tbl-cap: Plant superiority contrasts (paired Wilcoxon; 8 pairs each).
fmt_contrast("plant_superiority.csv")
fmt_contrast("plant_superiority_motility.csv")
```

## 6. Diagnostics, sensitivity and refits

Three diagnostics were run. First, rank-test validity: several contrasts
contain tied absolute differences (all five *congolense* dose contrasts;
most motility contrasts, whose endpoint averages nine binary points) or
dropped zero differences (superiority: one of eight pairs; several low-dose
motility pairs with n_nonzero as low as 4). Because the exact Wilcoxon
distribution is invalid with tied ranks, every contrast records `n_nonzero`,
`n_ties` and `p_method`, using exact p-values only when clean and the
continuity-corrected normal approximation otherwise — this refit left all
conclusions unchanged. Second, paired-difference symmetry (@fig-sym):
*evansi* differences sit entirely below zero (a location shift,
unproblematic); superiority differences spread symmetrically around zero,
matching its null. Third, leave-one-block-out sensitivity (@tbl-loo): no
single block flips any conclusion (evansi top doses LOO p = 0.016
throughout; superiority LOO p 0.53–1.0). Completeness is enforced
structurally at build (row counts and part levels asserted).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-loo
#| tbl-cap: Leave-one-block-out sensitivity (stable = no single block flips the conclusion).
k("sensitivity_loo.csv")
```

![Paired differences: symmetry check (red = median)](`r file.path(fig_dir, "diagnostic_paired_diffs.png")`){#fig-sym}

## 7. Discussion

The three assay layers tell one coherent story. In-vitro, both plants kill in
a strictly ordered, concentration-dependent manner (@fig-tti, @tbl-mot-dose);
in-vivo, the same ordering reappears in peak parasitaemia (@tbl-peak),
mortality (@fig-mort) and cumulative burden (@fig-auc), with 100 mg/ml
suppressing peaks to zero and eliminating deaths in both parasites. The
convergence of motility TTI gradients and AUC gradients is the study's
strongest internal replication: fast kill in the dish predicts low burden in
the mouse. Against this consistency stand two nulls. First, the plants are
interchangeable: superiority pairs split 4–3 with one exact tie across
parasites and parts (@fig-forest), chemistry overlaps heavily (universal
Saponin/Carbohydrates/Tannins, equal leaf richness of 6/12; §5.2), and
neither endpoint separates them — so objective v is answered negatively, and
the part-specific differentiating compounds (Steroids, Terpenoids and the
like) show no efficacy signature at this resolution. Second, weight and PCV
carry no treatment signal at all (@tbl-other), which exonerates the
parasitaemia findings from toxicity confounding while confirming *T.
congolense* as the more pathogenic parasite (all flag categories concentrate
there). The main asymmetry is parasite dose sensitivity: *T. evansi* yields
to 0.5 mg/ml (Holm 0.039) where *T. congolense* responds only at 100 mg/ml
and suggestively (Holm 0.071) — yet overall burdens do not differ
(p = 0.46), so this is a threshold difference, not a virulence difference.
The caveats from §2 and §6 bound every claim: group-mean data, N = 8 per
contrast, unknown controls, and death-censored AUCs read strictly alongside
mortality. Within those bounds, the supported thesis statement is narrow and
firm: both extracts are active in a dose-dependent manner with 100 mg/ml
fully suppressive, *T. evansi* the more sensitive parasite, and neither
plant demonstrably superior.

## 8. Limitations

Group means of n = 3 mice erase within-group variance, so inference rests on
N = 16 blocks — power is low, intervals wide, description carries the
weight. Control identities/doses are unknown; Positive Control is a validity
reference only. Death-censored AUC flatters early-death groups, hence AUC is
always read with mortality. NA = death is conventional, worth confirming
against animal records. All results are exploratory, not confirmatory.
